items.prompt: Decide whether this function is tail recursive.

let rec mystery (l : bool list) : bool =
  begin match l with
  | [] -> true
  | hd :: tl -> hd && mystery tl
  end
items.key: Tail recursive (the recursive call is the right operand of &&, which is in tail position).

items.prompt: Decide whether this function is tail recursive.
items.code:
let rec mystery (l : 'a list) (f : 'a -> 'a) : 'a =
  begin match l with
  | [] -> failwith "error"
  | hd :: [] -> f hd
  | hd :: tl -> f (mystery tl f)
  end

items.prompt: This mystery sums f x + f (x-1) + ... + f 1 but is not tail recursive. Write a tail-recursive mystery with the same header that behaves the same on all inputs (it may loop where the original would overflow the stack).
items.notes: The exam fixes the header (name mystery, same arguments); a local helper is allowed. The key adds f x, f (x-1), ... in the opposite grouping from the original, which gives the same result because integer addition (with wraparound) is associative and commutative. It also calls f in a different order than OCaml's usual right-to-left evaluation of the original, which only matters if f has side effects. For negative x both versions never reach 0, which the prompt allows. The outer 'rec' is unused (warning only), but the exam supplies that line.

        | None -> (* which edge case? *)

items.key:
let split_deque (d : 'a deque) (x : 'a) : 'a deque * 'a deque =
  let rec loop (dno : 'a dqnode option) : 'a deque * 'a deque =
    begin match dno with
    | None -> (d, create ())
    | Some n ->
      if n.v = x then
        begin match n.prev with
        | None -> (create (), d)
        | Some p ->
          let d2 = {head = dno; tail = d.tail} in
          d.tail <- n.prev;
          p.next <- None;
          n.prev <- None;
          (d, d2)
        end
      else loop n.next
    end
  in loop d.head
items.notes: Matches the skeleton: three update lines plus a return value. None covers both an empty d and x not found, and (d, create ()) handles both. n.prev = None means x is at the head, so the answer is (empty, d). create () is the Homework 4 empty-deque constructor.

items.prompt: After let a = {y = None}, let b = {y = Some a}, let c = b, say whether each expression is true or false (== is reference equality, = is structural equality). Picture: a points to record A (y = None); b and c both point to record B, whose y points to a Some cell holding A.
items.code:
type t = {mutable y : t option}
let a : t = {y = None}
let b : t = {y = Some a}
let c : t = b

1. a == b
2. a = b
3. b == c
4. b = c
5. c.y == Some a
6. c.y = Some a
7. (begin match c.y with
    | None -> None
    | Some d -> d.y
    end) = None
items.key:
1. a == b: False
2. a = b: False
3. b == c: True
4. b = c: True
5. c.y == Some a: False
6. c.y = Some a: True
7. (match c.y ... Some d -> d.y) = None: True
items.notes: Item 5 is false because 'Some a' allocates a new Some cell. Item 7 evaluates to a.y = None, so it is true.

items.prompt: Starting from an empty stack and heap, run the code and draw the resulting ASM stack and heap.
items.key: Stack: a, b, c, d, each pointing to its own record. a.y now points at a fresh Some cell → d; the heap is a cycle a → d → c → b → a (each record's Some cell points to the previous record).
items.notes: Concretely: B.y → Some → A, C.y → Some → B, D.y → Some → C, and A.y → (new) Some → D. The phrase 'points to the previous record' fits b, c and d. For a it means the previous record around the cycle (d), not a record defined earlier.

items.prompt: Starting from an empty stack and heap, run the code and draw the resulting ASM stack and heap.
items.code:
type t = {mutable y : t option}
let a : t = {y = Some {y = None}}
;; begin match a.y with
   | None -> ()
   | Some b -> b.y <- a.y
   end
let b : t option = a.y
items.key: the inner record X has X.y <- a.y, the same Some cell S that a holds; S → X, so X.y → S → X, a two-node cycle. Stack: a → A; b → S (the same Some cell as a.y).
items.notes: The b bound inside the match is temporary and is not on the final stack. The top-level b has type t option, so it points to the Some cell S, not to a record.

let make_game (init_pos : int) : widget =
  let pos = {contents = init_pos} in
  let circle_drawing (g : Gctx.gctx) : unit =
    Gctx.draw_ellipse g (pos.contents, 10) 5 5 in
  let board, canvas_nc = canvas (100, 20) circle_drawing in
  let (left_w, left_lc, left_nc) = button "Left" in
  let left () = pos.contents <- max (pos.contents - 1) 5 in
  left_nc.add_event_listener (mouseclick_listener left);
  (* line 10: Right button and listener, omitted by the exam *)
  let full_game = hlist [board; border left_w; border right_w] in
  border full_game
items.notes: Every graded blank (lines 2, 4, 6, 8, 9) comes from the guide. The guide's '...' tail was replaced with lines 11–12, copied from the exam (page 11), not made up. Line 10 is omitted in the exam itself and has no blanks, so the Right-button code is left out and its bound is not specified. 'ref init_pos' and '!pos' are equivalent to the record-field forms.

items.prompt: Implement isSubArray(small, big, row, col), which checks whether the m x m array small appears in big with its top-left corner at (row, col). Then use it in numberOfAppearances, which counts the (possibly overlapping) occurrences of small in the n x n array big, where 0 < m <= n. Example: small = [[1,1],[2,2]] and big = [[1,1,9,9],[2,2,9,9],[9,1,1,1],[9,2,2,2]] gives 3.
items.notes: isSubArray assumes the caller keeps row + m <= n and col + m <= n, which the loop bounds in numberOfAppearances guarantee. On the example the key returns 3, at (0,0), (2,1) and (2,2).
